[abstract] This study investigates whether English-tuned abliteration of refusal behaviour transfers to Slovene in two sibling 12B Gemma-3 checkpoints.

[abstract] Across four iterations and fifteen experiments, we find that the cross-lingual transfer of weight edits depends on where in the layer stack the edit energy lands, not on how many layers it covers or how much total energy it applies.

[abstract] The causal write profile, which measures which layers mediate refusal when edited one at a time, peaks at layer 19 in the English-centric anchor and layer 27 in the Slovene-specialised sibling, and the overlap between the profile and an edit's energy distribution orders refusal outcomes at Spearman above 0.83 in both checkpoints.
[abstract] However, the overlap instrument fails its primary criterion (incremental R-squared over log-energy is only 0.026 in the anchor) and fails on argmax-band prediction in the sibling.
[abstract] Two cheap one-forward-pass baselines outperform the expensive causal profile.

[abstract] Separately, Heretic's keyword-based selection objective is structurally blind in the low-refusal region of the anchor model (gradient-blind fraction 47% among candidates with classifier refusal at most 50%), explaining why the anchor search produced an under-optimised edit while the sibling search did not.

[abstract] Fourteen of the study's hypotheses were falsified, and the behavioural dissociation between the two models is bounded by achieved optimisation strength rather than by an inherent property of the model pair.
[abstract] Native-speaker review remains pending for 640 items across five packets.
[Framing] Abliteration removes refusal behaviour from language models by orthogonalising weight matrices against a "refusal direction" extracted from English harmful-vs-harmless contrasts [1].
[Framing] The procedure was introduced by Arditi et al.

[Framing] [1] and automated by tools such as Heretic, which uses TPE search over layer, position, direction index, and LoRA rank to find abliteration configurations that minimise an English refusal objective while bounding KL divergence from the original model.
[Framing] The question motivating this study is whether that English-centred objective leaves Slovene refusal behaviour uncontrolled.
[Framing] If the English refusal direction is universal across languages, as Wang et al.
[Framing] [2] report for safety-aligned models evaluated across 14 languages, then abliteration tuned on English should transfer to Slovene.
[Framing] If instead Slovene refusal relies partly on representations that the English objective does not observe, a gap will remain.

[Framing] The practical consequence is that a model abliterated to comply in English might still refuse in Slovene, or might lose Slovene capabilities that the English-only KL constraint does not protect.
[Framing] Several concurrent lines of work inform this question.
[Framing] BabelSteering [4] and Yoon et al.
[Framing] [5] show that safety alignment imposes disparate costs across languages, with non-English users bearing higher utility loss.

[Framing] [6] diagnose the breakdown point for low-resource safety as an action failure rather than a representation failure: the model encodes harmfulness correctly but fails to convert the representation into refusal.
[Framing] [7] formalise this as a disentangled safety hypothesis, separating a recognition axis from an execution axis.
[Framing] On the abliteration side, Fafula [8] documents off-target effects of refusal removal across model families, and Young [14] and Petrov [15] compare abliteration methods across architectures.
[Framing] Upadhyaya and Sikdar [9] analyse how safety and language identity become entangled, while Hawkins et al.
[Framing] [10] show that benign multilingual fine-tuning has heterogeneous safety impacts.
[Framing] Labunets [11] demonstrates that refusal geometry reflects refusal training diversity.
[Framing] On quantisation effects relevant to our NF4 setup, Marchisio et al.
[Framing] [12] and Chimoto et al.
[Framing] [13] show that quantisation calibration language matters for multilingual performance.
[Framing] [16] identify language-specific neurons, and Ghussin et al.
[Framing] [17] propose principled layer selection for multilingual steering.
[Framing] Frank [18] argues that refusal-based alignment evaluation conflates detection with routing.

[Framing] We study this question in a controlled bilingual setting using two sibling 12B models from the Gemma-3 family: google/gemma-3-12b-it (the English-centric reference) and cjvt/GaMS3-12B-Instruct (a Slovene continual-pretraining and SFT variant of the same architecture).
[Framing] Both are loaded in bnb_4bit NF4 quantisation throughout.
[Framing] The study proceeds in four iterations.
[Framing] Iteration 1 runs matched Heretic abliteration on both models, screens for cross-language refusal-direction transfer, and builds the shared bilingual evaluation dataset.

[Framing] Iteration 2 uses that dataset to measure the surrogacy gap (what English outcomes fail to predict about Slovene), test causal mechanisms, and evaluate safety and utility on held-out benchmarks.
[Framing] Iteration 3 tests the depth-coverage hypothesis, corrects Heretic's keyword objective, and extends the depth-redundancy index to additional models and languages.
[Framing] Iteration 4 measures the causal write profile in both models, tests the overlap instrument, quantifies gradient blindness of the keyword objective, and audits all prior claims.
